title: Mother and son again, 1861
hook: after long years apart, Duleep meets his mother, and she tells him of his heritage
carry: she told him who he was

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elveden, and your line was far from punjab. Today, someone arrives who remembers.

What do you say to a mother you last saw when you were small? A hotel in Calcutta. A grown man in English clothes waits in a room. The door opens, and a woman comes in, older than he remembers, her eyesight failing. She is Maharani Jind Kaur, the queen who was sent away. When she reaches him, the story goes, she runs her hands over his head, looking for his uncut hair, and finds it cut short.
screen: `A HOTEL IN CALCUTTA.` → `A QUEEN WHOSE EYES ARE FAILING.` → `HER HANDS ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: After she was separated from her son, Jind Kaur was held as a prisoner. She escaped in disguise and made her way to Nepal, where she lived in exile under the protection of its rulers. All those years, letters between mother and son were watched or stopped. Duleep Singh asked to see her, and in time the British allowed it, as long as she did not go back to the Punjab. They met in Calcutta. The boy she had last held was now a grown man, a Christian, living as an English gentleman. She came with him to England and lived near him in London. She talked to him about the Punjab, about his father, Ranjit Singh, about the kingdom and how it was lost, and about the Sikh faith he had been raised away from. Histories that follow his life mark this as the moment something in him began to turn. There's a hymn of Guru Arjan in which a mother speaks to her son: this is your mother's blessing, son, that you never forget the Lord for even an instant. That blessing is about remembering the Lord. In Calcutta, and then in London, this mother's gift was a remembering too: she gave her son back the story of who he was.
screen: `AN ESCAPE TO NEPAL.` · `A MEETING IN CALCUTTA.` · `STORIES OF THE PUNJAB.` · `A MOTHER'S BLESSING.` · then, large: `SHE TOLD HIM WHO HE WAS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your mother, a grandparent, or any elder who knew you when you were small: their face, their hands, the sound of their voice, and what they told you about where you come from. If they're living, think of one question you'd like to ask them; if they've died, think of one thing they told you that you'd like to keep. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru for a few breaths.
Asees, blessing, a mother's blessing to her son never to forget the Lord: Jind Kaur and Duleep Singh, meeting in Calcutta after long years apart. Today's word.
Your line: she told him who he was. Some of the best gifts are stories. Day nine hundred forty-three.
